title: After Talks Until 4 AM, BRICS Reaches Consensus With India's Help
excerpt: Negotiators hammered out a joint declaration condemning unilateral war after all-night consultations led by India, bridging deep divisions between Iran and the UAE over the Gulf conflict.
body:
• BRICS countries reached consensus on a joint declaration after negotiations continued until 4 am on Saturday, hours before leaders met in New Delhi.
  • India led the overnight consultations, bridging deep divisions between Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE over the Gulf conflict.
  • The declaration is expected to condemn unilateral war by any country without naming any country, four sources told Reuters.
  • Leaders including China's Xi Jinping, Russia's Vladimir Putin, and Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian gathered in New Delhi for the weekend summit.

BRICS countries reached consensus on a joint declaration in the early hours of Saturday, capping marathon negotiations that continued until 4 am as host India worked to reconcile members deeply divided over the Gulf conflict. The breakthrough, reported by ANI, clears the way for the bloc's leaders to approve the declaration at the summit in New Delhi this weekend. The deal matters because the expanded grouping now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE — three West Asian powers with deep differences and competing positions — and finding language acceptable to all three was the summit's hardest diplomatic test.

Context & Background

BRICS has grown from its original five members to an 11-member grouping over the past two years, with the inclusion of Iran, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Ethiopia, and Indonesia. That expansion has complicated consensus-building: the forum now seats countries on opposite sides of live conflicts.

The friction point at this summit has been the Gulf conflict. The UAE announced an indefinite trade embargo on Iran on August 19, accusing Iranian forces of firing two ballistic missiles at its territory. Iran denied the allegation, calling the reported attack a "false flag operation" by Israel and the United States.

This is not the first time the divide has paralyzed the grouping. At a BRICS foreign ministers' meeting in New Delhi in May, members failed to agree on contentious language about the conflict, and India had to fall back on issuing a Chair's statement. Ahead of the summit, an Indian official said the goal was not to eliminate differences but to find formulations acceptable to all and prevent geopolitical disputes from derailing the agenda.

"India's approach was to be 'very transparent and inclusive,' allowing every member to put forward its views while identifying areas where consensus could be built."

— Indian official, quoted in The Hindu BusinessLine

India led sustained consultations with member countries to reconcile the competing positions, and the talks reportedly continued until 4 am on Saturday before consensus emerged, paving the way for the joint statement.

Impact & Analysis

The emerging formula for the declaration — condemning unilateral war by any country while naming none — is classic diplomatic compromise. Reuters reported that negotiators had settled on that approach, with the leaders expected to approve the document later on Saturday. Foreign policy experts cautioned that such a statement was unlikely to shift the geopolitical landscape, but said it would demonstrate unity among emerging nations pushing back against measures such as Western sanctions.

"The key test for the bloc would be finding language on the Middle East crisis that both Abu Dhabi and Tehran could accept."

— Foreign policy analysts, speaking to Reuters

Beyond the declaration, the summit carries broader signals. Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in New Delhi on Saturday for his first visit to India in seven years, a marker of a thaw between the bloc's two largest members. Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa, and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan are also attending.

The bloc's economic agenda runs in parallel: cross-border payments, deeper economic cooperation, and reform of the World Bank, IMF, and WTO — institutions several members view as dominated by Western powers.

Diaspora Angle

For Indians abroad, the Gulf dimension of this story hits close to home. The UAE and Saudi Arabia are among the largest destinations for Indian workers and professionals overseas, and millions of Indian families depend on remittance corridors and travel routes across the region. A negotiated path that keeps Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE talking inside the same forum — rather than hardening into open confrontation — directly serves the safety and livelihoods of the Indian diaspora in the Gulf. It also burnishes India's standing as a bridge between competing powers, giving the diaspora a more influential India at the table when global rules on trade, payments, and migration are written.

What's Next

The leaders are expected to formally approve the declaration on Saturday. The full text will be scrutinized for what it says — and deliberately avoids saying — about the Gulf conflict and the reform of global institutions. The May foreign ministers' meeting showed how quickly Iran-UAE tensions can block joint language; this weekend's deal suggests the expanded BRICS can still function when a host works through the night.
